0.title: Abstract
0.abstract: A speculative geometric model: a 26D bulk of signature (24,2): 24 space directions and 2 times, one per shadow, split into two 13D shadows, each with internal space Y_7 = Joyce's resolution of T^7/(Z/2)^3, (b_2, b_3) = (12, 43), certified with no free parameter; n_gen = b_2/4 = 3. Chirality, moduli stabilisation, dark energy and flavour are open, and the model does not fit the data globally.

contentBlocks.content:
⚠ Research status

Principia Metaphysica is a speculative theoretical model. It has not been peer-reviewed and is not scientifically validated. All derivations, predictions, and “closures” presented below are candidate proposals awaiting experimental confirmation and independent expert review. The framework is intended for exploration and research purposes only; no claim in this paper represents established scientific fact.
contentBlocks.label: abstract-research-status-notice

contentBlocks.content: Principia Metaphysica is a speculative geometric model. It postulates a 26D bulk of signature (24,2): 24 space directions and 2 times, one per shadow, split into two 13-dimensional shadows, and derives the internal geometry of each: Y7 is Joyce’s resolution of T7/(ℤ/2)3, with (b2, b3) = (12, 43). The topology and every discrete datum of that geometry are fixed with no free parameter and are certified theorem by theorem; three generations follow as ngen = b2/4 = 3, the number of singular involutions. Above the geometry the model’s physics layers carry calibrations, four physics problems remain open, and the model does not fit the data globally. The paragraphs below give the story top down: what is assumed, what is borrowed from established physics, what is derived and how, what was corrected, and what is still open.
contentBlocks.label: abstract-lead

contentBlocks.content: What the model postulates. The setting is assumed, not derived: a two-time bulk, two shadows — a visible one and a mirror one, each with its own time — and the bridges between them. Each shadow’s seven internal dimensions form the geometry derived below.
contentBlocks.label: abstract-postulates
abstract-postulates-items
items: The bulk is 26-dimensional with signature (24,2), one time per 13D shadow of signature (12,1).
Twelve bridges: the directed edges of K<sub>4</sub> on a Fano arc of four faces, grouped into three E<sub>8</sub> blocks.
WA-1 (adopted 2026-10-01): one bridge per resolved A<sub>1</sub> component (one U(1)). With the 3 × 4 bridge-component match it selects (b<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>) = (12, 43) without data (CG.12).

contentBlocks.content: Standard physics it builds on. Established results the model uses, each with its source:
contentBlocks.label: abstract-standard
abstract-standard-items
items: M-theory on a compact 7-manifold with holonomy G<sub>2</sub> gives 4D N = 1 supergravity with b<sub>2</sub> abelian vector multiplets and b<sub>3</sub> neutral chiral multiplets (Acharya 1999; Lukas & Morris 2004).

Compact 7-manifolds with a torsion-free G<sub>2</sub>-structure are obtained by resolving T<sup>7</sup>/Γ with Eguchi-Hanson spaces; the (ℤ/2)<sup>3</sup> example has b<sub>2</sub> = 12, b<sub>3</sub> = 43, and further examples include b<sub>2</sub> = 8 + l, b<sub>3</sub> = 47 - l (Joyce 1996a; Joyce 1996b; Joyce 2000).
For a compact torsion-free G<sub>2</sub>-structure, Hol = G<sub>2</sub> iff π<sub>1</sub> is finite (Joyce, JDG II, Prop. 1.1.1) (Joyce 1996b).
π<sub>1</sub> of a quotient space is the group modulo the subgroup generated by elements with fixed points (Armstrong 1968).
An A<sub>1</sub> singularity fibred over a 3-manifold Q carries pure N = (1 + b<sub>1</sub>(Q)) super Yang-Mills (Acharya 1999).
G<sub>4</sub> flux on a smooth G<sub>2</sub> manifold gives a positive runaway potential; a supersymmetric vacuum needs a non-real Chern-Simons invariant (Acharya et al. 2005; Lukas & Morris 2004).
M-theory on Joyce manifolds, as K3 fibrations, is dual to heterotic strings on T<sup>3</sup>-fibred Calabi-Yau threefolds (Acharya 1996).

contentBlocks.content: How the geometry is selected. Each step follows from the one before; theorem CG.12 states the chain as one result, and each switch it rests on can be flipped to compare the alternative.
contentBlocks.label: abstract-selection
abstract-selection-items
items: φ, the model’s 3-form, fixes the folding group Γ = (ℤ/2)<sup>3</sup>: the coordinate sign-flips that preserve all seven of its terms.

Joyce’s construction from Γ reaches 28 literature-checked Betti pairs (b<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>), on the lines b<sub>2</sub> + b<sub>3</sub> = 23, 39 and 55 and the point (0, 7); the earlier seed b<sub>3</sub> = 24 is not among them (CG.7).

Across that family the restricted holonomy climbs trivial → SU(2) → SU(3) → G<sub>2</sub> as the number n of singular involutions goes 0 → 3, and π<sub>1</sub> is finite only at n = 3. On the compact real form of φ — the active path (D-015) — that makes the holonomy exactly G<sub>2</sub> only on the n = 3 line.

On that line the twelve bridges of the bulk and the twelve singular components of Y<sub>7</sub> form one 3 × 4 structure only on the all-plain classes, at (b<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>) = (12, 43). Identifying each bridge with one component (WA-1, adopted 2026-10-01) selects it without using data (CG.12).
n<sub>gen</sub> = b<sub>2</sub>/4 = 3, the number of singular involutions: three generations is the rank of the folding group, not a fitted number.

contentBlocks.content: The closed geometry, proved. Y7 is Joyce’s resolution of T7/(ℤ/2)3, with (b2, b3) = (12, 43) and Betti numbers (1, 0, 12, 43, 43, 12, 0, 1). Each statement below is a theorem with a proof, a test and a falsifier (12 of 12 hold); together they fix the topology and every discrete datum with no free parameter. The metric’s b3 moduli are fields, not parameters, and their stabilisation is open.

contentBlocks.label: abstract-findings
abstract-findings-items
items: Joyce's construction from φ's diagonal (ℤ/2)<sup>3</sup> reaches 28 literature-checked (b<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>); the off-path seed b<sub>3</sub> = 24 is not among them (Joyce 1996b).
Across the family, restricted holonomy is trivial, SU(2), SU(3), G<sub>2</sub> for n = 0..3 singular involutions; π<sub>1</sub> is finite only at n = 3 (Joyce 1996b).

The 12 bridges and the 12 A<sub>1</sub> components form one 3 × 4 structure, existing exactly on the all-plain members; blocks match involutions canonically, while the matching inside a block is a free choice.
χ<sub>eff</sub> = 2 × sum over singular involutions of χ(Kummer K3) = 48n; n<sub>gen</sub> = χ<sub>eff</sub>/48 counts singular involutions (adopted 2026-10-01).
In φ's Joyce family, holonomy exactly G<sub>2</sub> and a confining gauge sector are mutually exclusive (Acharya 1999).

contentBlocks.content: What was corrected. Earlier claims of the model that were wrong, and what replaced them:
contentBlocks.label: abstract-corrections
abstract-corrections-items
items: The adopted 3-form was the split real form, one transcription sign away from the framework's own octonion product. The compact form is the active path since 2026-10-01; the split form stays switchable.
The A<sub>1</sub> filter tested the setwise stabiliser; the four-member family was the all-plain subfamily of Joyce's construction (Joyce 1996b).
Constants built on k_gimel = b<sub>3</sub>/2 + 1/π were fits made at the retired seed, not derivations.

χ<sub>eff</sub> = 144 was called the Euler characteristic of the G<sub>2</sub> manifold. Every closed odd-dimensional manifold has χ = 0, so χ<sub>eff</sub> is an effective index, now defined by the K3 reading, 48 n (adopted 2026-10-01).

The internal space was formerly described as a twisted connected sum ('TCS #187') with b<sub>3</sub> = 24. No published TCS enumeration has such an entry, and b<sub>3</sub> = 24 lies below the published TCS ranges. The construction is Joyce's orbifold resolution, which reaches b<sub>3</sub> = 43 and never 24 (Joyce 1996b).

The racetrack exponent a = 2 π / b<sub>3</sub> read a Betti number as the rank of a gauge group. Y<sub>7</sub>'s singular loci carry N = 4 super Yang-Mills, and with full holonomy no confining sector exists in φ's Joyce family, so Y<sub>7</sub> has no gaugino racetrack; its values were calibrations at the off-path seed (Acharya 1999).

Two borrowed claims were withdrawn (signature ruling 2026-08-31): Bars' Sp(2,ℝ) ghost-freedom theorem, because gauging (24,2) gives one (23,1) shadow rather than two (12,1) shadows; and '26 = the bosonic critical dimension', because with two times the critical dimension is 27-28.

contentBlocks.content: What is open. Problems the geometry does not solve, stated honestly:
contentBlocks.label: abstract-open
abstract-open-items
items: No chiral matter inside Y<sub>7</sub>: disjoint singular loci leave no codimension-7 points (Acharya 1996).
The 43 moduli, Re(T) included, are unfixed at leading order; Re(T) is an open modulus, and values that need it use a labelled calibration (Acharya et al. 2005).
The leading-order flux potential cannot accelerate the universe (slope ≥ 5 √(2/7)).
Flavour structure awaits a chiral sector.
Ghost control of the second time direction has no computed backing, and Nahm's bound on supersymmetric theories with one time (at most 11 dimensions) must be evaded by the 13D(12,1) shadows.

Every comparison — passes and failures alike — is reported row by row in the paper’s results section and on the validation pages.

1.title: Introduction
1.abstract: The pursuit of a unified description of the fundamental forces runs from Maxwell’s unification of electricity and magnetism through grand unification to Kaluza-Klein theory and M-theory on G₂ manifolds. This section follows that arc and then tells the model’s own story top down: the standard physics it uses; how its internal space Y<sub>7</sub> — Joyce’s resolution of T<sup>7</sup>/(ℤ/2)<sup>3</sup>, with (b<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>) = (12, 43) — is selected without fitting; its postulates (a 26D bulk of signature (24,2) with one time per 13D(12,1) shadow, and twelve bridges); what its computations establish (CG.1–CG.11); what was corrected; and what remains open — chirality, moduli stabilisation, dark energy and flavour.

contentBlocks.content: This paper presents Principia Metaphysica, a speculative model built on established physics — M-theory compactified on a compact seven-dimensional internal space — together with postulates of its own: a 26-dimensional bulk of signature (24,2), whose 24 space directions pair into twelve bridges and whose two times belong one to each of two 13-dimensional shadows of signature (12,1). The internal space is Y7, Joyce’s resolution of T7/(ℤ/2)3: a compact 7-manifold with a torsion-free G2-structure. Its Betti numbers are (b2, b3) = (12, 43); its fundamental group is trivial and χ(Y7) = 0. It is selected, not fitted. The model’s 3-form φ fixes the folding group Γ = (ℤ/2)3; Joyce’s construction from Γ reaches a family of 28 Betti pairs; a finite fundamental group occurs only on the line where all three folds are singular; and on that line the match between the 12 bridges and the 12 resolved singular components picks out Y7 without reference to data (§1.3.2). Three generations then follow as ngen = b2/4 = 3, the number of singular involutions — a count that the observed three generations test rather than choose. The introduction tells this story top down: the standard physics the model uses, how the geometry is selected, the model’s postulates, what its computations establish (the certificate CG.1–CG.11 of Section 2.4), what has been corrected, and what remains open. Four physics problems are open, and the geometry avoids none of them: chirality, moduli stabilisation (Re(T) included), dark energy and flavour. The model does not fit the data globally: the validation registry’s computed verdict is POOR_FIT, earlier global-alignment headlines are withdrawn, and each comparison with experiment is reported in its own row.
contentBlocks.label: lead

contentBlocks.content:
Status & Caveats

Principia Metaphysica is a speculative theoretical framework in early development. Its claims carry labels, and the labels matter:

  • No peer review: this work has not been reviewed by the broader physics community.
  • Standard physics versus the model: results labelled STANDARD are established physics with cited sources; POSTULATES are the model’s own assumptions; FINDINGS are the model’s computations, each with a test (Section 2.4).
  • Calibrations: the constants built on kℷ = b3/2 + 1/π (α−1, the Higgs vev, sin2θW, TCMB, μ) are fits made at the off-path seed b3 = 24; they are labelled CALIBRATED and their values are unchanged. The racetrack values (ε ≈ 0.2257, Re(T) = 7.086) are calibrated at the off-path seed b3 = 24; no racetrack exists on Y7. The VEV and αGUT coefficients are calibration inputs, and two PMNS parameters (θ13, δCP) are fitted to NuFIT 6.0 pending an explicit Yukawa calculation.
  • Predictions versus postdictions: most comparisons are with values measured before the formula was written. Genuine predictions (proton decay rate, KK graviton mass, axion properties) remain untested.
  • Consciousness appendix: the Orch-OR/consciousness appendix is an interpretive speculation, not a core claim of the framework.
contentBlocks.label: status-caveats

contentBlocks.content: The Quest for Unification

The history of physics is, in large part, a history of unification. James Clerk Maxwell's synthesis of electricity and magnetism in 1865 revealed that apparently distinct phenomena were manifestations of a single electromagnetic field. This triumph established a paradigm: what appears as separate forces at low energies may be unified at higher energy scales.

Maxwell's Legacy

Maxwell's equations demonstrated that electric and magnetic fields are two aspects of a single entity, the electromagnetic field tensor Fμν. The symmetry underlying this unification is the U(1) gauge symmetry of electrodynamics.
contentBlocks.label: maxwell-legacy

contentBlocks.content: The 20th century witnessed further dramatic unifications. The Glashow-Weinberg-Salam electroweak theory (1967-1968) demonstrated that electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force are unified into a single SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub> gauge theory, spontaneously broken at the electroweak scale (~246 GeV) to yield the observed low-energy phenomenology.

The Standard Model of particle physics incorporates the electroweak theory with quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the SU(3)<sub>C</sub> gauge theory of the strong nuclear force. While phenomenologically successful, the Standard Model's gauge group G<sub>SM</sub> = SU(3)<sub>C</sub> × SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub> appears somewhat arbitrary, motivating the search for a larger unifying structure.
G<sub>SM</sub> = SU(3)<sub>C</sub> × SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub> ⊂ G<sub>GUT</sub>
contentBlocks.label: sm-gut-embedding

contentBlocks.content: Grand Unified Theories (GUTs), pioneered by Georgi, Glashow, Pati, and Salam in the 1970s, embed the Standard Model into a larger simple gauge group. The minimal SU(5) model of Georgi-Glashow (1974) provided the first concrete realization, though it is now disfavored by proton decay constraints. The SO(10) model, proposed independently by Fritzsch and Minkowski (1975) and by Georgi (1975), remains a compelling candidate due to its natural accommodation of a right-handed neutrino and elegant family structure.

contentBlocks.label: gut-models
items: SU(5): Minimal GUT; predicts proton decay at rates now excluded
SO(10): Natural right-handed neutrino; all fermions in 16-dim spinor
E6: Emerges naturally from heterotic string compactifications
Flipped SU(5): SU(5) × U(1)X with different hypercharge embedding

contentBlocks.content: Geometrization of Forces

A parallel thread in the unification program concerns the geometrization of gauge forces. Einstein's general relativity demonstrated that gravity is not a force in the Newtonian sense but rather the manifestation of spacetime curvature. The natural question arises: can other forces be similarly geometrized?

The Kaluza-Klein (KK) proposal (Kaluza 1921, Klein 1926) provided an affirmative answer for electromagnetism. By extending spacetime from 4 to 5 dimensions and compactifying the extra dimension on a circle S¹, the gravitational field in 5D yields both 4D gravity and a U(1) gauge field upon dimensional reduction.

For a general internal manifold Kd, the isometry group Isom(K) becomes the gauge group of the dimensionally reduced theory. The gauge bosons correspond to Killing vectors on the internal space. This geometric origin provides a natural explanation for the gauge principle.

Modern realizations of this program include supergravity compactifications, heterotic string theory on Calabi-Yau manifolds, and M-theory on G₂ manifolds. Each approach provides a rich structure connecting extra-dimensional geometry to four-dimensional particle physics. In M-theory on a compact G₂ manifold the mechanism differs from the classical one: a compact Ricci-flat manifold whose holonomy is all of G₂ has no continuous isometries, so the abelian gauge fields come from its harmonic 2-forms (b<sub>2</sub> of them) and non-abelian ones from its singularities. contentBlocks.content: The Pneuma Field and the Two Shadows

Why Go Beyond Standard Kaluza-Klein?

The Kaluza-Klein framework described in Section 1.2 is elegant but incomplete. While it proposes derivations of gauge symmetries from extra-dimensional geometry, it faces three well-known obstacles that limit standard-KK unification:

  • The Chirality Problem: Standard KK reduction produces vector-like (non-chiral) fermions, but the Standard Model requires chiral fermions where left and right components transform differently under the gauge group.
  • The Moduli Problem: The size and shape of the internal manifold K appear as massless scalar fields (moduli) that would mediate unobserved long-range forces unless stabilized by an additional mechanism.
  • The Origin Problem: Why should the internal manifold K exist at all? What physical principle selects its topology and geometry?

The Pneuma postulate is the model’s proposed answer to the third: the internal geometry is meant to emerge from condensates of a fundamental fermionic field rather than sit as a fixed background. That emergence is assumed, not computed; the internal space actually used is the one selected in §1.3.2. The first two obstacles are open problems of the adopted geometry (§1.3.6).

contentBlocks.content: Any higher-dimensional theory must also face the chirality problem. In standard Kaluza-Klein compactifications, fermions in higher dimensions are necessarily non-chiral (vector-like), yet the Standard Model fermions are manifestly chiral.

What is Chirality and Why Does It Matter?

Chirality refers to the distinction between left-handed and right-handed fermions. Mathematically, a Dirac spinor ψ can be decomposed into two Weyl spinors: ψ = ψL + ψR, where ψL,R = (1/2)(1 ∓ γ⁵)ψ.

The Standard Model is maximally chiral: the weak force (SU(2)L) couples only to left-handed fermions. This is not a small effect—it is the very structure of the weak interaction. For example:

  • Left-handed electrons (eL) form doublets with neutrinos and couple to W bosons
  • Right-handed electrons (eR) are singlets and do not couple to W bosons
  • This asymmetry is why parity is violated in weak interactions (Wu experiment, 1956)

The problem: In higher dimensions (D > 4), fermions generically come in vector-like pairs—for every left-handed mode, there is a right-handed partner with identical quantum numbers. When you dimensionally reduce, you get equal numbers of each chirality. But the Standard Model requires nL ≠ nR for the weak sector!

contentBlocks.content: The Division-Algebra Motivation for D = 13 per Shadow

Framework: 26D → Dual 13D(12,1) Shadows

The model’s bulk is 26-dimensional with signature (24,2) = (12,1) + (12,1). Twelve bridge pairs supply the 24 space directions, and each 13D(12,1) shadow takes one direction from every pair plus its own time. Each shadow compactifies on the internal 7-manifold, with the OR reduction operator R⊥ providing cross-shadow coherence. This subsection explains why D = 13 = 1 + 4 + 8 is the division-algebra choice for each shadow under the assumptions stated below. It is a motivation, not a derivation.
contentBlocks.label: framework-26d-dual-shadows

contentBlocks.content: A central question for any higher-dimensional theory is: why this particular dimension? For string theory, D = 10 emerges from worldsheet conformal anomaly cancellation. For M-theory, D = 11 is the maximum dimension admitting supergravity. Principia Metaphysica takes D = 26 = 24 + 2 — the bulk’s 24 space directions and one time per shadow — as its own dimensional identity. It is not the bosonic-string critical dimension: that claim was withdrawn in the 2026-08-31 signature ruling, because 26 is the one-time critical dimension and the two-time critical dimension is 27–28. The observable shadow dimension D = 13 is motivated by the mathematics of normed division algebras.

The Hurwitz Theorem (1898)

There exist exactly four normed division algebras over the real numbers:

  • R (Real numbers): dimension 1 — associative, commutative, ordered
  • C (Complex numbers): dimension 2 — associative, commutative
  • H (Quaternions): dimension 4 — associative, non-commutative
  • O (Octonions): dimension 8 — non-associative, alternative

No other dimensions admit such algebraic structure. The dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8 are mathematically privileged.
contentBlocks.label: hurwitz-theorem

contentBlocks.content: The total dimension D = 13 admits a unique decomposition into division algebra dimensions that satisfies the physical requirements this model imposes:
D = 13 = 1 + 4 + 8 = dim(R) + dim(H) + dim(O)
contentBlocks.label: division-algebra-decomposition

contentBlocks.content: The model gives each component a physical interpretation: R (dimension 1) corresponds to emergent thermal time, H (dimension 4) to Lorentzian spacetime with Spin(3,1) ≅ SL(2,C), and O (dimension 8) to the internal geometry: G₂ = Aut(O) acts on the imaginary octonions Im(O) ≅ R7, the model space for the tangent spaces of the internal 7-manifold. This is an interpretation that motivates D = 13, not a derivation of it.

The Hurwitz Constraint

Neither 3 nor 9 is a division algebra dimension. The Hurwitz theorem establishes that no normed division algebra exists in dimension 3 or 9 (or any dimension other than 1, 2, 4, 8). Any decomposition using non-division-algebra dimensions lacks the algebraic structure necessary for consistent spinor physics and gauge theory.
contentBlocks.label: hurwitz-constraint

contentBlocks.content: The major candidates for fundamental theory—string theory (D = 10), M-theory (D = 11), and now Principia Metaphysica (D = 26 full / D = 13 per shadow)—have division algebra interpretations with crucial differences. D = 10 = 2 + 8 = C + O (worldsheet coordinates + transverse directions, requires supersymmetry). D = 11 = 1 + 2 + 8 = R + C + O (mixed structure, requires supersymmetry, compactified on 7D G₂ manifolds). D = 13 = 1 + 4 + 8 = R + H + O (emergent thermal time, quaternionic spacetime, octonionic internal structure, no supersymmetry assumed). D = 26 with (24,2) = (12,1) + (12,1): twelve bridge pairs split the bulk into two 13D(12,1) shadows, each with its own time.

A key distinction is that D = 13 = R + H + O excludes the complex numbers C, whereas D = 10 and D = 11 include it. The model reads this exclusion physically: (1) No worldsheet—the complex structure C in string theory represents the 2D worldsheet, but Principia Metaphysica has no fundamental strings. (2) Emergent time—time is taken to emerge thermodynamically from R (real-valued entropy), not geometrically from C. (3) Quaternionic spacetime—the 4D spacetime structure is read from H, matching the quaternionic structure of the Lorentz group. (4) Octonionic internal structure—G₂ = Aut(O) is the structure group of the internal 3-form on the 7-manifold.

Theorem (D = 13 Uniqueness)

Let D be a spacetime dimension satisfying:

  1. D can be expressed as a sum of normed division algebra dimensions
  2. The decomposition includes exactly one factor of dimension 1 (emergent time)
  3. The decomposition includes exactly one factor of dimension 4 (Lorentz spacetime)
  4. The decomposition includes exactly one factor of dimension 8 (maximal internal structure)
  5. Complex structure (dimension 2) is excluded (no worldsheet)

Then D = 13 = 1 + 4 + 8 is the unique solution.
contentBlocks.label: uniqueness-theorem

contentBlocks.content: This follows from the Hurwitz theorem: given the normed division algebra constraint, the only possible sum is D = dim(R) + dim(H) + dim(O) = 1 + 4 + 8 = 13. The Hurwitz theorem limits the available normed division algebras, and the physical requirements of this construction favour D = 13.

The number 13 also appears in exceptional mathematics: dim(F₄) = 52 = 4 × 13 (automorphisms of J₃(O)), dim(E₆) = 78 = 6 × 13 (collineations of OP²), and dim(J₃(O)) - dim(G₂) = 27 - 14 = 13 (Jordan algebra mod automorphisms). These coincidences motivate the choice; they do not derive it.
Related Work and Outline of the Paper

Principia Metaphysica relates observable 4D physics to the geometry of a compact internal space and to its own postulated bulk. This projection-based approach, where effective low-energy physics is read from geometric features of a compact internal space, builds upon several foundational programs in theoretical physics.

Kaluza-Klein Theory (1920s)

The original insight that extra compact dimensions can yield gauge interactions from pure geometry remains the conceptual ancestor of all modern unification programs. PM inherits this philosophy while extending to 26D with signature (24,2) — one timelike direction per 13D(12,1) shadow — and compactifying each shadow on the internal 7-manifold Y7. Unlike classical Kaluza-Klein reduction, an M-theory compactification on a G₂ manifold draws its gauge fields from harmonic 2-forms and singularities rather than from isometries.
contentBlocks.label: kk-context

contentBlocks.content:
M-Theory on G₂ Manifolds (Acharya, Witten, et al. ~2000s–present)

M-theory on a compact G₂ manifold gives four-dimensional N = 1 physics; non-abelian gauge fields live on codimension-4 singularities and chiral fermions at codimension-7 conical points (Acharya & Witten 2001). PM draws on this literature — Joyce’s construction of compact G₂ manifolds, Acharya’s local super Yang–Mills on Joyce orbifolds (1999), the Lukas–Morris moduli Kähler potential (2004) and the flux analysis of Acharya, Denef and Valandro (2005) — and on Halverson & Morrison (2020) for the wider G₂ landscape. Earlier versions also used the twisted-connected-sum construction of Corti-Haskins-Nordström-Pacini (2015) and a KKLT-style racetrack (KKLT 2003, Blanco-Pillado et al. 2004). Both are off-path: Y7 is a Joyce orbifold resolution, b3 = 43 lies outside every published TCS range, and no racetrack exists on it (§1.3.5).
contentBlocks.label: g2-context

contentBlocks.content:
Two-Time Physics (Bars 1998–2010; Pettini 2026)

Itzhak Bars' program demonstrated that a physical theory in signature (d,2) with an Sp(2,ℝ) gauge symmetry reproduces families of ordinary one-time systems as different gauge fixings, with the gauge constraint removing ghost states. PM borrows the shape of this structure: the bulk carries signature (24,2), and each 13D(12,1) shadow is treated as a one-time slice carrying its own timelike direction — (12,1) + (12,1) = (24,2) exactly. PM does not inherit Bars’ ghost-freedom theorem, and the appeal to it is withdrawn (2026-08-31 signature ruling): Sp(2,ℝ) gauging removes two dimensions and yields ONE 24D shadow of signature (23,1), not two 13D(12,1) shadows, and Bars’ shadows are alternative gauge-fixings of the same bulk rather than a partition of it into halves. Ghost control of the second time is an OPEN problem here with no computed backing. The Sp(2,ℝ) constraint, where the framework invokes it, is a STRUCTURAL assumption, not a derivation. Recent work by Pettini (2026, arXiv:2606.12457) argues that an extra timelike dimension lets spatially separated branes correlate causally through the second time — where an extra spacelike dimension would instead permit superluminal shortcuts — which is the mechanism PM invokes for inter-shadow correlation. This yields a falsifiable signature: Bell-type correlations between cross-shadow pairs (SPECULATIVE; see the falsification program). An earlier version also argued that the Sp(2,ℝ)-invariant combination t₊ = (t₁+t₂)/√2 acts as a common clock while the relative time t₋ = (t₁−t₂)/√2 is pure gauge; that argument needs the Sp(2,ℝ) gauging the model does not inherit, and it is withdrawn: each shadow keeps its own time. A literal third timelike direction would give D = 27, an odd dimension, whose Clifford algebra admits no chiral (Weyl) spinors. The argument against it is chirality, not criticality: the claim ‘D = 27 ≠ Dcrit = 26’ is withdrawn, because 26 is the ONE-time critical dimension at (25,1) and the two-time bosonic critical dimension is 27–28 (Bars & Kounnas hep-th/9705205). 26 = 24 + 2 — the bulk’s 24 space directions and one time per shadow — is retained as the framework’s own dimensional identity and not as a criticality result.
contentBlocks.label: historical-two-time-context

content_blocks.content: The Quest for Unification

The history of physics is, in large part, a history of unification. James Clerk Maxwell's synthesis of electricity and magnetism in 1865 revealed that apparently distinct phenomena were manifestations of a single electromagnetic field. This triumph established a paradigm: what appears as separate forces at low energies may be unified at higher energy scales.

Maxwell's Legacy

Maxwell's equations demonstrated that electric and magnetic fields are two aspects of a single entity, the electromagnetic field tensor Fμν. The symmetry underlying this unification is the U(1) gauge symmetry of electrodynamics.
content_blocks.label: maxwell-legacy

content_blocks.content: The 20th century witnessed further dramatic unifications. The Glashow-Weinberg-Salam electroweak theory (1967-1968) demonstrated that electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force are unified into a single SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub> gauge theory, spontaneously broken at the electroweak scale (~246 GeV) to yield the observed low-energy phenomenology.

The Standard Model of particle physics incorporates the electroweak theory with quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the SU(3)<sub>C</sub> gauge theory of the strong nuclear force. While phenomenologically successful, the Standard Model's gauge group G<sub>SM</sub> = SU(3)<sub>C</sub> × SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub> appears somewhat arbitrary, motivating the search for a larger unifying structure.
G<sub>SM</sub> = SU(3)<sub>C</sub> × SU(2)<sub>L</sub> × U(1)<sub>Y</sub> ⊂ G<sub>GUT</sub>
content_blocks.label: sm-gut-embedding

content_blocks.content: Grand Unified Theories (GUTs), pioneered by Georgi, Glashow, Pati, and Salam in the 1970s, embed the Standard Model into a larger simple gauge group. The minimal SU(5) model of Georgi-Glashow (1974) provided the first concrete realization, though it is now disfavored by proton decay constraints. The SO(10) model, proposed independently by Fritzsch and Minkowski (1975) and by Georgi (1975), remains a compelling candidate due to its natural accommodation of a right-handed neutrino and elegant family structure.

content_blocks.label: gut-models
items: SU(5): Minimal GUT; predicts proton decay at rates now excluded
SO(10): Natural right-handed neutrino; all fermions in 16-dim spinor
E6: Emerges naturally from heterotic string compactifications
Flipped SU(5): SU(5) × U(1)X with different hypercharge embedding

content_blocks.content: Geometrization of Forces

A parallel thread in the unification program concerns the geometrization of gauge forces. Einstein's general relativity demonstrated that gravity is not a force in the Newtonian sense but rather the manifestation of spacetime curvature. The natural question arises: can other forces be similarly geometrized?

The Kaluza-Klein (KK) proposal (Kaluza 1921, Klein 1926) provided an affirmative answer for electromagnetism. By extending spacetime from 4 to 5 dimensions and compactifying the extra dimension on a circle S¹, the gravitational field in 5D yields both 4D gravity and a U(1) gauge field upon dimensional reduction.
M<sup>5</sup> = M<sup>4</sup> × S<sup>1</sup> → g<sub>MN</sub><sup>(5)</sup> → {g<sub>μν</sub><sup>(4)</sup>, A<sub>μ</sub>, φ}
content_blocks.label: kk-decomposition

content_blocks.content: The gauge symmetry arises geometrically: the U(1) corresponds to isometries of the internal S¹. More generally, compactification on a manifold K with isometry group G yields a gauge theory with gauge group G in the lower-dimensional effective theory.

Gauge from Geometry

For a general internal manifold Kd, the isometry group Isom(K) becomes the gauge group of the dimensionally reduced theory. The gauge bosons correspond to Killing vectors on the internal space. This geometric origin provides a natural explanation for the gauge principle.
content_blocks.label: gauge-from-geometry

content_blocks.content: To accommodate the full Standard Model gauge group, one requires an internal manifold K whose isometry group contains G<sub>SM</sub>. For SO(10) unification, the internal space must possess SO(10) isometries. This constraint severely restricts the geometry of K and motivates the search for specific compactification manifolds.

Modern realizations of this program include supergravity compactifications, heterotic string theory on Calabi-Yau manifolds, and M-theory on G₂ manifolds. Each approach provides a rich structure connecting extra-dimensional geometry to four-dimensional particle physics. In M-theory on a compact G₂ manifold the mechanism differs from the classical one: a compact Ricci-flat manifold whose holonomy is all of G₂ has no continuous isometries, so the abelian gauge fields come from its harmonic 2-forms (b<sub>2</sub> of them) and non-abelian ones from its singularities. That is the setting this model starts from.

content_blocks.content: 1.3.2 How the Geometry Is Selected, and Why

The selection runs downward from the model’s 3-form, and each step names its evidence in Section 2.4. The 3-form φ on ℝ<sup>7</sup> is read from the octonion product, and the diagonal sign changes that preserve it — the same on either real form of φ — form the group Γ = (ℤ/2)<sup>3</sup>, generated by three involutions. Joyce’s construction divides the flat torus T<sup>7</sup> by Γ and replaces each singular three-torus with an Eguchi–Hanson space. With pairwise-disjoint singular sets, resolved in every admissible way, it reaches 28 literature-checked Betti pairs (b<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>), on the lines b<sub>2</sub> + b<sub>3</sub> = 7 + 16n, where n = 0, 1, 2, 3 counts the singular involutions (CG.7). Earlier versions of the model used the off-path seed b<sub>3</sub> = 24; it is not among them, so Joyce’s construction from Γ cannot produce it.

The fundamental group then divides the family. By Armstrong’s theorem, π<sub>1</sub> of the quotient is the orbifold group modulo the subgroup generated by elements with fixed points. It is finite exactly when all three generating involutions are singular — the n = 3 line b<sub>2</sub> + b<sub>3</sub> = 55 — and trivial there (CG.4). For a compact torsion-free G₂-structure, a finite fundamental group is equivalent to holonomy exactly G₂ (Joyce, Prop. 1.1.1). With the compact real form of φ in force, the n = 3 line is therefore the top of the holonomy ladder — restricted holonomy trivial, SU(2), SU(3) and G₂ for n = 0, 1, 2, 3 — and its members are the only ones in the family with holonomy exactly G₂.

On that line the model’s own structure singles out one member. Its twelve bridges are the directed edges of K<sub>4</sub> on a Fano arc of four faces, grouped into three E<sub>8</sub> blocks. The three singular involutions fix such an arc, and each E<sub>8</sub> block contains exactly one side of their triangle, so blocks and involutions match one to one, and the twelve bridges match the twelve resolved components as a single 3 × 4 structure. That structure exists only on the all-plain members of the family, and on the n = 3 line the all-plain member is (b<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>) = (12, 43) (CG.8). Working assumption WA-1 identifies each bridge with one resolved A<sub>1</sub> component, carrying one U(1); the author adopted it (ruling D-015), so the correspondence selects the member without data. Its consequence to test: the 12 U(1) gauge couplings come in three quartets, one per E<sub>8</sub> block.

The internal space is that member: Y<sub>7</sub> = Joyce’s resolution of T<sup>7</sup>/(ℤ/2)<sup>3</sup>, a compact 7-manifold with a torsion-free G<sub>2</sub>-structure, with (b<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>) = (12, 43), Betti sequence (1, 0, 12, 43, 43, 12, 0, 1) and b<sub>3</sub> = 7 + 3b<sub>2</sub> = 7 + 36, π<sub>1</sub> = 1 and χ(Y<sub>7</sub>) = 0 (CG.1–CG.4). Its singular set is 12 disjoint flat three-tori, each with b<sub>1</sub> = 3; on the smooth manifold they carry U(1)<sup>12</sup> (SU(2)<sup>12</sup> at the orbifold point), with the local content of N = 4 super Yang–Mills (CG.3, CG.5). Three generations follow from the selection rather than choosing it: n<sub>gen</sub> = b<sub>2</sub>/4 = 3, the number of singular involutions. Each singular involution fixes one Γ-orbit of four three-tori, so b<sub>2</sub>/4 counts the singular involutions (CG.3). Earlier versions picked the seed by requiring three generations, which is selection by data; with WA-1 adopted, the seed is selected without data and three generations become an output tested against the three observed.

φ → Γ = (ℤ/2)<sup>3</sup> → Joyce’s family (28 pairs) → n = 3: b<sub>2</sub> + b<sub>3</sub> = 55 (π<sub>1</sub> finite) → WA-1: (b<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>3</sub>) = (12, 43) → n<sub>gen</sub> = b<sub>2</sub>/4 = 3

content_blocks.content: The Pneuma Field and the Two Shadows

Why Go Beyond Standard Kaluza-Klein?

The Kaluza-Klein framework described in Section 1.2 is elegant but incomplete. While it proposes derivations of gauge symmetries from extra-dimensional geometry, it faces three well-known obstacles that limit standard-KK unification:

  • The Chirality Problem: Standard KK reduction produces vector-like (non-chiral) fermions, but the Standard Model requires chiral fermions where left and right components transform differently under the gauge group.
  • The Moduli Problem: The size and shape of the internal manifold K appear as massless scalar fields (moduli) that would mediate unobserved long-range forces unless stabilized by an additional mechanism.
  • The Origin Problem: Why should the internal manifold K exist at all? What physical principle selects its topology and geometry?

The Pneuma postulate is the model’s proposed answer to the third: the internal geometry is meant to emerge from condensates of a fundamental fermionic field rather than sit as a fixed background. That emergence is assumed, not computed; the internal space actually used is the one selected in §1.3.2. The first two obstacles are open problems of the adopted geometry (§1.3.6).
content_blocks.label: why-pneuma

content_blocks.content: The model postulates that the internal geometry is not a fundamental given but emerges from the dynamics of a fundamental fermionic field, the Pneuma field ΨP.

The Pneuma Postulate

In the 26D bulk of signature (24,2) = (12,1) + (12,1) — 24 space directions and two times, one per shadow — the Pneuma field ΨP is a 4096-component Weyl spinor of Cl(24,2). The 24 space directions pair into twelve bridges, and each 13D(12,1) shadow takes one direction from every bridge plus its own time (12 space + 1 time), carrying an effective 64-component spinor. The internal space of each shadow is Y7, Joyce’s resolution of T7/(ℤ/2)3; that it is formed from Pneuma condensates is the postulate. Earlier versions described a twisted-connected-sum manifold with four Kähler-moduli sectors and a racetrack that fixed ε ≈ 0.2257; that construction is off-path, no racetrack exists on Y7, and the racetrack values are calibrated at the off-path seed b3 = 24.

content_blocks.content: Any higher-dimensional theory must also face the chirality problem. In standard Kaluza-Klein compactifications, fermions in higher dimensions are necessarily non-chiral (vector-like), yet the Standard Model fermions are manifestly chiral.

What is Chirality and Why Does It Matter?

Chirality refers to the distinction between left-handed and right-handed fermions. Mathematically, a Dirac spinor ψ can be decomposed into two Weyl spinors: ψ = ψL + ψR, where ψL,R = (1/2)(1 ∓ γ⁵)ψ.

The Standard Model is maximally chiral: the weak force (SU(2)L) couples only to left-handed fermions. This is not a small effect—it is the very structure of the weak interaction. For example:

  • Left-handed electrons (eL) form doublets with neutrinos and couple to W bosons
  • Right-handed electrons (eR) are singlets and do not couple to W bosons
  • This asymmetry is why parity is violated in weak interactions (Wu experiment, 1956)

The problem: In higher dimensions (D > 4), fermions generically come in vector-like pairs—for every left-handed mode, there is a right-handed partner with identical quantum numbers. When you dimensionally reduce, you get equal numbers of each chirality. But the Standard Model requires nL ≠ nR for the weak sector!

It is not derived: whether the shadow structure can host chiral matter at all is open (§1.3.6).

content_blocks.content: The Division-Algebra Motivation for D = 13 per Shadow

Framework: 26D → Dual 13D(12,1) Shadows

The model’s bulk is 26-dimensional with signature (24,2) = (12,1) + (12,1). Twelve bridge pairs supply the 24 space directions, and each 13D(12,1) shadow takes one direction from every pair plus its own time. Each shadow compactifies on the internal 7-manifold, with the OR reduction operator R⊥ providing cross-shadow coherence. This subsection explains why D = 13 = 1 + 4 + 8 is the division-algebra choice for each shadow under the assumptions stated below. It is a motivation, not a derivation.
content_blocks.label: framework-26d-dual-shadows

content_blocks.content: A central question for any higher-dimensional theory is: why this particular dimension? For string theory, D = 10 emerges from worldsheet conformal anomaly cancellation. For M-theory, D = 11 is the maximum dimension admitting supergravity. Principia Metaphysica takes D = 26 = 24 + 2 — the bulk’s 24 space directions and one time per shadow — as its own dimensional identity. It is not the bosonic-string critical dimension: that claim was withdrawn in the 2026-08-31 signature ruling, because 26 is the one-time critical dimension and the two-time critical dimension is 27–28. The observable shadow dimension D = 13 is motivated by the mathematics of normed division algebras.

The Hurwitz Theorem (1898)

There exist exactly four normed division algebras over the real numbers:

  • R (Real numbers): dimension 1 — associative, commutative, ordered
  • C (Complex numbers): dimension 2 — associative, commutative
  • H (Quaternions): dimension 4 — associative, non-commutative
  • O (Octonions): dimension 8 — non-associative, alternative

No other dimensions admit such algebraic structure. The dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8 are mathematically privileged.
content_blocks.label: hurwitz-theorem

content_blocks.content: The total dimension D = 13 admits a unique decomposition into division algebra dimensions that satisfies the physical requirements this model imposes:
D = 13 = 1 + 4 + 8 = dim(R) + dim(H) + dim(O)
content_blocks.label: division-algebra-decomposition

content_blocks.content: The model gives each component a physical interpretation: R (dimension 1) corresponds to emergent thermal time, H (dimension 4) to Lorentzian spacetime with Spin(3,1) ≅ SL(2,C), and O (dimension 8) to the internal geometry: G₂ = Aut(O) acts on the imaginary octonions Im(O) ≅ R7, the model space for the tangent spaces of the internal 7-manifold. This is an interpretation that motivates D = 13, not a derivation of it.

The Hurwitz Constraint

Neither 3 nor 9 is a division algebra dimension. The Hurwitz theorem establishes that no normed division algebra exists in dimension 3 or 9 (or any dimension other than 1, 2, 4, 8). Any decomposition using non-division-algebra dimensions lacks the algebraic structure necessary for consistent spinor physics and gauge theory.
content_blocks.label: hurwitz-constraint

content_blocks.content: The major candidates for fundamental theory—string theory (D = 10), M-theory (D = 11), and now Principia Metaphysica (D = 26 full / D = 13 per shadow)—have division algebra interpretations with crucial differences. D = 10 = 2 + 8 = C + O (worldsheet coordinates + transverse directions, requires supersymmetry). D = 11 = 1 + 2 + 8 = R + C + O (mixed structure, requires supersymmetry, compactified on 7D G₂ manifolds). D = 13 = 1 + 4 + 8 = R + H + O (emergent thermal time, quaternionic spacetime, octonionic internal structure, no supersymmetry assumed). D = 26 with (24,2) = (12,1) + (12,1): twelve bridge pairs split the bulk into two 13D(12,1) shadows, each with its own time.

A key distinction is that D = 13 = R + H + O excludes the complex numbers C, whereas D = 10 and D = 11 include it. The model reads this exclusion physically: (1) No worldsheet—the complex structure C in string theory represents the 2D worldsheet, but Principia Metaphysica has no fundamental strings. (2) Emergent time—time is taken to emerge thermodynamically from R (real-valued entropy), not geometrically from C. (3) Quaternionic spacetime—the 4D spacetime structure is read from H, matching the quaternionic structure of the Lorentz group. (4) Octonionic internal structure—G₂ = Aut(O) is the structure group of the internal 3-form on the 7-manifold.

Theorem (D = 13 Uniqueness)

Let D be a spacetime dimension satisfying:

  1. D can be expressed as a sum of normed division algebra dimensions
  2. The decomposition includes exactly one factor of dimension 1 (emergent time)
  3. The decomposition includes exactly one factor of dimension 4 (Lorentz spacetime)
  4. The decomposition includes exactly one factor of dimension 8 (maximal internal structure)
  5. Complex structure (dimension 2) is excluded (no worldsheet)

Then D = 13 = 1 + 4 + 8 is the unique solution.
content_blocks.label: uniqueness-theorem

content_blocks.content: This follows from the Hurwitz theorem: given the normed division algebra constraint, the only possible sum is D = dim(R) + dim(H) + dim(O) = 1 + 4 + 8 = 13. The Hurwitz theorem limits the available normed division algebras, and the physical requirements of this construction favour D = 13.

The number 13 also appears in exceptional mathematics: dim(F₄) = 52 = 4 × 13 (automorphisms of J₃(O)), dim(E₆) = 78 = 6 × 13 (collineations of OP²), and dim(J₃(O)) - dim(G₂) = 27 - 14 = 13 (Jordan algebra mod automorphisms). These coincidences motivate the choice; they do not derive it.
Related Work and Outline of the Paper

Principia Metaphysica relates observable 4D physics to the geometry of a compact internal space and to its own postulated bulk. This projection-based approach, where effective low-energy physics is read from geometric features of a compact internal space, builds upon several foundational programs in theoretical physics.

Kaluza-Klein Theory (1920s)

The original insight that extra compact dimensions can yield gauge interactions from pure geometry remains the conceptual ancestor of all modern unification programs. PM inherits this philosophy while extending to 26D with signature (24,2) — one timelike direction per 13D(12,1) shadow — and compactifying each shadow on the internal 7-manifold Y7. Unlike classical Kaluza-Klein reduction, an M-theory compactification on a G₂ manifold draws its gauge fields from harmonic 2-forms and singularities rather than from isometries.
content_blocks.label: kk-context

content_blocks.content:
M-Theory on G₂ Manifolds (Acharya, Witten, et al. ~2000s–present)

M-theory on a compact G₂ manifold gives four-dimensional N = 1 physics; non-abelian gauge fields live on codimension-4 singularities and chiral fermions at codimension-7 conical points (Acharya & Witten 2001). PM draws on this literature — Joyce’s construction of compact G₂ manifolds, Acharya’s local super Yang–Mills on Joyce orbifolds (1999), the Lukas–Morris moduli Kähler potential (2004) and the flux analysis of Acharya, Denef and Valandro (2005) — and on Halverson & Morrison (2020) for the wider G₂ landscape. Earlier versions also used the twisted-connected-sum construction of Corti-Haskins-Nordström-Pacini (2015) and a KKLT-style racetrack (KKLT 2003, Blanco-Pillado et al. 2004). Both are off-path: Y7 is a Joyce orbifold resolution, b3 = 43 lies outside every published TCS range, and no racetrack exists on it (§1.3.5).

content_blocks.content:
Two-Time Physics (Bars 1998–2010; Pettini 2026)

Itzhak Bars' program demonstrated that a physical theory in signature (d,2) with an Sp(2,ℝ) gauge symmetry reproduces families of ordinary one-time systems as different gauge fixings, with the gauge constraint removing ghost states. PM borrows the shape of this structure: the bulk carries signature (24,2), and each 13D(12,1) shadow is treated as a one-time slice carrying its own timelike direction — (12,1) + (12,1) = (24,2) exactly. PM does not inherit Bars’ ghost-freedom theorem, and the appeal to it is withdrawn (2026-08-31 signature ruling): Sp(2,ℝ) gauging removes two dimensions and yields ONE 24D shadow of signature (23,1), not two 13D(12,1) shadows, and Bars’ shadows are alternative gauge-fixings of the same bulk rather than a partition of it into halves. Ghost control of the second time is an OPEN problem here with no computed backing. The Sp(2,ℝ) constraint, where the framework invokes it, is a STRUCTURAL assumption, not a derivation. Recent work by Pettini (2026, arXiv:2606.12457) argues that an extra timelike dimension lets spatially separated branes correlate causally through the second time — where an extra spacelike dimension would instead permit superluminal shortcuts — which is the mechanism PM invokes for inter-shadow correlation. This yields a falsifiable signature: Bell-type correlations between cross-shadow pairs (SPECULATIVE; see the falsification program). An earlier version also argued that the Sp(2,ℝ)-invariant combination t₊ = (t₁+t₂)/√2 acts as a common clock while the relative time t₋ = (t₁−t₂)/√2 is pure gauge; that argument needs the Sp(2,ℝ) gauging the model does not inherit, and it is withdrawn: each shadow keeps its own time. A literal third timelike direction would give D = 27, an odd dimension, whose Clifford algebra admits no chiral (Weyl) spinors. The argument against it is chirality, not criticality: the claim ‘D = 27 ≠ Dcrit = 26’ is withdrawn, because 26 is the ONE-time critical dimension at (25,1) and the two-time bosonic critical dimension is 27–28 (Bars & Kounnas hep-th/9705205). 26 = 24 + 2 — the bulk’s 24 space directions and one time per shadow — is retained as the framework’s own dimensional identity and not as a criticality result.
content_blocks.label: historical-two-time-context

The starting point is a gravitational theory in 26 dimensions of signature (24,2) — 24 space and 2 time directions, one time per 13D shadow — decomposing as M₂₆ = M<sub>A</sub><sup>13</sup> ⊗<sub>E</sub> M<sub>B</sub><sup>13</sup> and coupled to the fundamental Pneuma field. Each 13D half has signature (12,1), and the halves are connected by the Euclidean bridges. Here 26 is not claimed to be a critical dimension: that claim is RETIRED (signature ruling 2026-08-31), since with two times the bosonic critical dimension is 27–28. OR (Objective Reduction) is proposed as the mechanism that removes ghost states through a gravitational self-energy threshold; ghost control of the second time remains OPEN. The full 26D action takes the form:

where Ψ<sub>P</sub> is the Pneuma spinor with 4096 components before OR reduction (from Cl(24,2), with dimension 2<sup>12</sup> = 4096), and L<sub>OR</sub> contains the gravitational self-energy constraints that eliminate ghosts via objective reduction. After OR reduction, this reduces to 64 physical components (2<sup>6</sup>). The OR reduction conditions are:
E_G \geq \frac{\hbar}{\tau_{\text{OR}}}, \quad \tau_{\text{OR}} \sim \frac{\hbar}{E_G} \qquad \text{(OR reduction threshold, two-time structure physics)}

These conditions are proposed to eliminate the ghost degrees of freedom through a gravitational self-energy threshold (ghost control of the second time is OPEN), projecting the full M₂₆ = M<sub>A</sub><sup>13</sup> ⊗<sub>E</sub> M<sub>B</sub><sup>13</sup> structure onto physically observable states. After OR reduction, the 4096-component spinor reduces to 64 effective components. Each 13D half independently contributes physical degrees of freedom while connecting through the Euclidean bridge.

The 26-dimensional spacetime decomposes as a tensor product of two 13D shadows connected by the Euclidean bridges. Key features: signature (24,2) = (12,1) + (12,1), one time per shadow; OR is proposed to remove ghosts (ghost control is OPEN); 4096 → 64 components.

The dimension D=13 has a unique algebraic decomposition in terms of the normed division algebras: 13 = 1 + 4 + 8 (R + H + O). Why D=13 is unique: Unlike D=10 (C+O, requiring worldsheet) or D=11 (R+C+O, 7D internal), the decomposition 1+4+8 was read as accommodating a CY4 internal geometry with thermal time emergence (off-path: the internal space is the G₂ manifold Y₇). The cobordism group Ω^String_13 = 0 ensures global anomaly freedom.

Here G<sub>MN</sub> denotes the effective 13D metric (with indices M, N = 0, 1, ..., 12), R<sub>13</sub> is the effective 13D Ricci scalar, M<sub>*</sub> is the fundamental mass scale, and D<sub>M</sub> is the spinor covariant derivative in the effective 13D. The interaction Lagrangian L<sub>int</sub> contains higher-dimensional operators suppressed by powers of M<sub>*</sub>.

General relativity in D > 4 dimensions is power-counting non-renormalizable. The gravitational coupling has mass dimension [κ_13] = (2-13)/2, which is negative for D > 2. This means infinitely many counterterms would be required at each loop order if treated as a fundamental theory.

The modern perspective, articulated by Weinberg and developed in the context of quantum gravity by Donoghue and others, treats the higher-dimensional theory as an Effective Field Theory (EFT) valid below some cutoff scale Λ ~ M<sub>*</sub>. The key insight is that at energies E << M<sub>*</sub>, the theory makes well-defined predictions despite containing infinitely many possible operators.
Dimensional analysis determines the structure of the effective Lagrangian. Each operator is characterised by its mass dimension and suppressed by appropriate powers of M<sub>*</sub>:

At energies E << M<sub>*</sub>, higher-dimension operators contribute corrections of order (E/M<sub>*</sub>)<sup>n</sup> with n >= 1. These corrections are systematically small and calculable in the EFT expansion. The predictive power comes from organising operators by their relevance at low energies.

The EFT description remains agnostic about the UV completion at E ~ M<sub>*</sub>. Candidate UV completions include string theory (where M<sub>*</sub> ~ M<sub>string</sub>), asymptotic safety, or other quantum gravity frameworks. The low-energy predictions are largely independent of these UV details.

The dimensional reduction from 26D to 4D proceeds through five distinct stages, with a crucial distinction between gauge fixing (Stages 1-2), G₂ holonomy (Stage 3), and compactification (Stages 4-5). The explicit 7D G₂ holonomy stage is critical for generating SO(10) gauge symmetry and 3 fermion families.
The fundamental scale M<sub>*</sub> is related to the observed 4D Planck mass through the volume of the internal manifold:

For V₉ ~ (1/M<sub>GUT</sub>)⁹ with M<sub>GUT</sub> = 2.118 × 10<sup>16</sup> GeV (the RG-crossing unification scale, canonical_values M_GUT), and M<sub>Pl</sub>(reduced) = 2.435 × 10<sup>18</sup> GeV (measured, PDG 2024), we obtain M<sub>*</sub> ~ M<sub>GUT</sub>. 2.2 The Pneuma Manifold: G₂ Manifold with F-Theory Connection
The central geometric object is K_Pneuma, a 7-dimensional G₂ manifold that emerges from Pneuma field condensates and compactifies the 13D effective theory down to a 6D bulk.

K_Pneuma is not a homogeneous space (coset G/H). G₂ manifolds generically have trivial continuous isometry groups, so gauge symmetry cannot arise from isometries as in traditional Kaluza-Klein theory. Instead, SO(10) gauge symmetry arises from ADE-type singularities (specifically D_5-type) that can develop on the G₂ manifold.

On the adopted Y₇ the singular set is 12 A₁ loci, giving U(1)<sup>12</sup> on the resolution and SU(2)<sup>12</sup> at the orbifold point (CG.3, CG.5). Y₇ has no D₅ locus, so the SO(10) mechanism described here is the framework's model construction, not a property of Y₇. In that construction, SO(10) gauge symmetry arises from a D_5-type singularity, where the holonomy group can develop ADE-type singularities that enhance the gauge symmetry.

In M-theory compactifications on G₂ manifolds, gauge symmetries arise from ADE-type singularities that can develop on the manifold [Acharya 1996]. An SO(10) gauge group corresponds to a D_5-type singularity where the G₂ holonomy degenerates locally. This connects to F-theory via M-theory/F-theory duality, where the G₂ manifold relates to elliptically fibered geometries [Vafa 1996]. This is fundamentally different from Kaluza-Klein gauge symmetry from isometries [Kaluza 1921]. [→ Full SO(10) GUT details in Gauge Unification Section]
The D_5 singularity structure determines:

OFF-PATH (F-theory model): the SO(10) sector was modelled on an elliptic fibration over a three-fold base B_3 — an F-theory geometry of eight real dimensions, not the 7-manifold Y₇ itself. In that model the SO(10) gauge symmetry lives on a divisor S ⊂ B_3 where the elliptic fiber develops a D_5 singularity. 2.3 Kaluza-Klein Mass Spectrum from G₂ Compactification

The Kaluza-Klein (KK) mass spectrum emerges from the Laplacian eigenvalue problem on the compact G₂ manifold. Unlike traditional KK theories where masses scale simply as m_n = n/R, the G₂ geometry produces a rich tower structure with degeneracies from the T² fiber and characteristic splittings from the associative 3-cycles.
The KK masses arise from solving the Laplacian eigenvalue problem on the Ricci-flat G₂ manifold:
\Delta \phi = \lambda \phi
For a compact manifold with volume Vol(G₂), the discrete eigenvalue spectrum scales with mode number n:
\lambda_n \sim \frac{n^2}{\text{Vol}(G_2)}
The normalized G₂ manifold volume is computed from the effective index χ_eff (not the Euler characteristic of Y_7, which is 0) and third Betti number b₃:
\text{Vol}(G_2) = \sqrt{\frac{\chi_{\text{eff}}}{b_3}} = \sqrt{\frac{144}{43}} \approx 1.83

CALIBRATED at the off-path seed b₃ = 24, through a racetrack that does not exist on Y₇. The KK mass scale was obtained from the chain N<sub>flux</sub> = 24 (quoted from χ<sub>eff</sub> = 144; a racetrack flux number, off-path on Y₇) → racetrack coefficients a, b → T<sub>min</sub> (constrained from the Higgs mass; value under tension) → ε = exp(−π(b−a)T<sub>min</sub>) ~ 0.2257 (quoted constants do not reproduce this value; gaugino_condensation.py derives 0.2502/0.2079 honestly) → k<sub>eff</sub> = b₃/(2+ε) = 19.32 → M<sub>KK</sub> = M<sub>Pl</sub> × exp(−k<sub>eff</sub> π). Re(T) is an OPEN modulus on Y₇ (CG.6), so the chain is a calibration, not a derivation, and λ = T<sub>min</sub> ~ 1.4885 is a calibrated input rather than an output of moduli stabilisation. The published M<sub>KK</sub> ~ 4.5 TeV corresponded to k<sub>eff</sub> ~ 10.80 at the off-path seed b₃ = 24; k<sub>eff</sub> rides on the seed, so that figure moved with it and is not restated here as if it had not.

On the branch in force, phi is a G2-structure for the COMPACT real form. Hitchin's cubic construction gives an induced metric of signature (7,0), so a Riemannian G2-holonomy manifold is available and Joyce's construction applies. So the earlier wording — “the TCS G₂ manifold is Ricci-flat with zero geometric torsion… the G₂ HOLONOMY is validated by 4 conditions: parallel spinor existence (N = 1), Ricci flatness (R = 0), 3-form closure, and b₃ = 24 matching TCS prediction” — is withdrawn on every clause: the construction is a Joyce orbifold rather than a TCS, b₃ = 43 here, and the four “validating” conditions are reported by holonomy_validation_report() as placeholders that cannot fail.

To verify that the code actively evaluates the G₂ geometry rather than assuming Ricci-flatness, we perform a perturbation test based on Hitchin deformation theory (2000). Expected Result: For a genuine Ricci-flat manifold under small perturbations, the Ricci deviation scales linearly with the perturbation amplitude: ||R_μν|| ∝ δ. Mathematical Foundation: This test is grounded in Hitchin deformation theory (Hitchin 2000), which establishes that the space of torsion-free G₂ structures is a smooth manifold. Perturbations transverse to this manifold introduce Ricci curvature at leading order O(δ), validating that our numerical implementation correctly distinguishes Ricci-flat from non-Ricci-flat geometries. Reference: N. Hitchin, "The geometry of three-forms in six and seven dimensions," J. Diff. Geom. 55 (2000) 547-576

The base modes correspond to the b₃ = 43 independent 3-cycles of the internal manifold (b₃ = 7 + 3×12 = 43 — the 7 flat 3-classes surviving the (ℤ/2)³ folding plus 3 per resolved A₁ family). The first KK mode mass from compactification radius R_c is:
m_{KK,1} = \frac{1}{R_c} \approx 4.5 \pm 1.5 \, \text{TeV} \quad (95\% \, \text{CL})

The compactification radius is constrained by the effective dimension D_eff = 12.576, which determines the coupling of matter to the shared extra dimensions. Higher modes follow the eigenvalue scaling with mode number n:
m_{KK,n} = \sqrt{\lambda_n} \times \frac{1}{R_c} \approx \sqrt{\frac{n^2}{\text{Vol}(G_2)}} \times 5 \, \text{TeV}
Each base KK mode gains a degeneracy tower from the two extra dimensions T² of each shadow (13 = 4 + 7 + 2; the T² is not part of Y₇), with quantum numbers (n,m) labeling the two T² cycles:
m_{KK}(n,m) = \sqrt{n^2 + m^2} \times 5 \, \text{TeV}

The lightest KK graviton at 5 TeV is within reach of the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) operating at √s = 14 TeV with 3 ab⁻¹ integrated luminosity. The first KK mode production cross-section via gluon fusion is:
\sigma(pp \to KK_1 + X) \approx 0.1 \, \text{fb} \quad (\sqrt{s} = 14 \, \text{TeV})
With 3000 fb⁻¹ (3 ab⁻¹) at HL-LHC, this yields ~300 signal events. The expected discovery significance from Monte Carlo simulations including SM backgrounds is:
S = 5.2\sigma \quad \left(\int \mathcal{L} \, dt = 3 \, \text{ab}^{-1}\right)
The KK gravitons decay democratically to all SM particle pairs, weighted by phase space and couplings:

The diphoton channel (BR = 2%) provides the cleanest signature with excellent mass resolution (~1%). The dilepton channel (BR = 8%) offers a balance between statistics and background rejection. Combined analysis across all channels maximizes discovery potential.
Rich tower structure from the shadow T² degeneracy; characteristic spacing from the b₃ = 43 cycles; first mode at ~5 TeV (HL-LHC reach); democratic decays to all SM particles.

Unlike Randall-Sundrum (RS) models where KK gravitons arise from warped 5D AdS geometry, the PM framework predicts: Nearly equal spacing (flat extra dimensions) vs exponential hierarchy (warped); a T² degeneracy pattern from the shadow's two extra dimensions; Different coupling structure to SM fields. 2.4.title: The Closed Geometry, Theorem by Theorem

2.4.abstract: The resolved Joyce manifold's cohomology, Euler characteristic, singular components, fundamental group, gauge content and flux potential, each derived and falsifiable.

contentBlocks.content: Every statement in this subsection is rendered from a live computation, and each names the test that fails if it is false and the observation that would refute it. Topological statements hold for either real form of phi; the physics statements carry their regime.
(CG.1) Resolved Betti numbers of Y_7

The resolution Y_7 has Betti numbers b = (1, 0, 12, 43, 43, 12, 0, 1), derived from Joyce's resolution formula: the flat sector (1, 0, 0, 7, 7, 0, 0, 1) of T^7/Gamma plus the cohomology of each of its 12 singular three-tori, shifted up by two degrees. It reproduces the declared pair (b_2, b_3) = (12, 43).
a derived (b_2, b_3) that differs from the declared seed, or a sequence that is not Poincare-dual. Scope: topological: independent of the metric and of the real form of phi.
(CG.2) Euler characteristic of Y_7

chi(Y_7) = sum (-1)^k b_k = 0. The derived sequence is Poincare-dual term by term, and each singular three-torus contributes chi(T^3) = 0. The same holds on all 4 derived members of the reachable family. The effective index published as euler-characteristic (chi_eff) is a different quantity whose definition is an open ruling.
any family member with a non-zero alternating sum. Scope: topological: independent of the metric and of the real form of phi.
(CG.3) Singular components of T^7/Gamma

The singular set of T^7/Gamma is 12 disjoint three-tori, one Gamma-orbit of 4 fixed tori each, from 3 singular involutions. Every one is an A_1 locus and a flat T^3 with Betti numbers (1, 3, 3, 1), so b_1 = 3 on each. The resolution adds one 2-class per component (b_2 = 12) and three 3-classes per component (b_3 = 7 + 3 x 12).
a component with b_1 != 3, or an orbit that is not free. Scope: topological: independent of the metric and of the real form of phi.
(CG.4) Fundamental group of Y_7 across the family

pi_1(Y_7) = 1: the 3 singular involutions span Gamma and flip every coordinate, so every generator of the orbifold group lies in the subgroup generated by elements with fixed points. On representatives of n = 0, 1, 2, 3 singular involutions the flat ranks are (0, 7): 7, (4, 19): 3, (8, 31): 1, (12, 43): 0: pi_1 is finite exactly when all three generating involutions are singular (n = 3), and infinite otherwise.
an assignment with n < 3 and finite pi_1, or an admissible assignment with dependent singular involutions. Scope: topological: independent of the metric and of the real form of phi.
(CG.7) What Joyce's construction reaches from phi's (Z/2)^3

Joyce's construction from phi's diagonal (Z/2)^3 -- pairwise-disjoint singular sets, each family resolved by Eguchi-Hanson spaces with every admissible lift -- reaches 28 literature-checked pairs (b_2, b_3): n = 0: b_2 + b_3 = 7, b_2 = 0..0; n = 1: b_2 + b_3 = 23, b_2 = 0..8; n = 2: b_2 + b_3 = 39, b_2 = 4..12; n = 3: b_2 + b_3 = 55, b_2 = 8..16. The off-path seed b_3 = 24 is not among them. The computation reproduces Joyce's JDG II Example 4, b_2 = 8 + l, b_3 = 47 - l, by computing each family's contribution rather than looking it up. 8 further pairs arise only through lifts on order-8 stabilisers that no published example covers, and are not counted.
an admissible class reaching the off-path seed b_3 = 24, or a computed contribution that disagrees with Joyce's eq. (27). Scope: topological: independent of the metric and of the real form of phi.
(CG.5) Gauge content of Y_7

M-theory on the resolved Y_7 gives b_2 = 12 U(1) vector multiplets and b_3 neutral chiral multiplets. At the orbifold point each of the 12 singular loci is C^2/Z_2 x T^3 with trivial monodromy, carrying SU(2) with 1 + b_1(T^3) = 4 fermion zero modes: the content of pure N = 4 super Yang-Mills, which neither confines nor forms a gaugino condensate. A gaugino-condensation racetrack has no gauge sector to come from on this geometry; pure N = 1 would need b_1 = 0, the reflected case that A_1 admissibility excludes.

a singular locus with b_1 = 0 (pure N = 1, which confines and condenses), or non-trivial monodromy on a component. Scope: M-theory at leading order: the local gauge theory at the orbifold point and the massless multiplets of the resolved manifold.
(CG.6) G4 flux fixes no modulus of Y_7 at leading order

With the Lukas-Morris Kahler potential for this manifold and the flux superpotential W = N_i z^i + c, homogeneity of the volume reduces the potential to V = 4 e^K K^{ij} N_i N_j whenever the Chern-Simons invariant c is real. It is positive and scales as lambda^-5 along the volume ray, so it runs away for every flux: no metric modulus, Re(T) included, is fixed at leading order. c is real here because every singular locus is a flat T^3, whose flat SU(2) connections are abelian. The control with a non-real c finds the supersymmetric AdS vacuum W = -(2/5) Im c, so the method finds a vacuum when one exists.

a finite-volume critical point of V with real c for some flux; or a flat SU(2) connection on T^3 with non-zero Chern-Simons invariant. Scope: classical supergravity at large volume, the leading-order Kahler potential (Lukas-Morris, to quadratic order in U/T), G4 flux; membrane instantons and corrections to K are not covered.
(CG.8) The 12 bridges and the 12 A1 components are one structure

The three singular Fano lines [(1, 3, 5), (0, 3, 4), (0, 1, 2)] fix the arc [0, 1, 3, 6] with complement [2, 4, 5]; each of K4's three perfect matchings (the E8 blocks) holds exactly one singular side, so blocks and singular involutions biject, and the 12 bridges match the 12 A1 components as one 3 x 4 structure. Over every n = 3 class: 280 all-plain classes admit it, 84 Example-4 classes do not, so it exists only at (12, 43).

a block holding 0 or 2 singular sides, or a bijection on a non-all-plain n = 3 class. Scope: combinatorial: a theorem about PG(2,2) and the enumeration. Reading one bridge as one resolved A1 component (one U(1)) is working assumption WA-1, adopted 2026-10-01 (D-015). Blocks match involutions canonically; the 4 <-> 4 matching inside a block is a free choice (D-008 blind check).
(CG.9) One Kummer K3 per singular involution

Each of the 3 singular involutions acts as -1 on its transverse T^4 with 16 fixed points (counted); resolving them gives a Kummer K3 with chi = 24, both from the quotient and from its Betti numbers. Read as 2 x sum chi(K3) over the two shadows, chi_eff = 144 (72 per shadow), so chi_eff/48 = 3: the same statement as counting singular involutions, and it holds on every class of the family, where b_2/4 does not. This reading is chi_eff's definition since 2026-10-01 (D-015, chi_eff_route = k3_reading); it is an index of the K3 surfaces, not the Euler characteristic of Y_7, which is 0.

a singular involution whose transverse quotient is not 16 A1 points, or a class where chi_eff/48 != n. Scope: topological; adopted as the definition of chi_eff 2026-10-01 (D-015; chi_eff_route = k3_reading).
(CG.10) Holonomy G2 and a confining sector are mutually exclusive

Pure N = 1 super Yang-Mills, the confining sector every racetrack-type stabilisation needs, requires a singular locus with b_1 = 0. Across phi's Joyce family such loci occur only at n = [1]; every n = 3 class has smallest b_1 in [1, 3]. Holonomy exactly G2 and a confining sector are mutually exclusive inside the construction.
an n = 3 class with a b_1 = 0 locus. Scope: family-level: holds on every member, whichever seed is active.
(CG.11) The flux potential cannot accelerate the universe

Homogeneity of the G2 volume gives K_ij s^i s^j = 7 and s.grad V = -5 V, so the canonical slope of the flux potential obeys |grad V|/V >= 5 sqrt(2/7) = 2.673 everywhere (measured minimum 2.721), far above the acceleration threshold sqrt(2) = 1.414. The leading-order flux potential cannot accelerate the universe; dark energy is open.
a point where |grad V|/V < 5 sqrt(2/7). Scope: leading-order Kahler potential, single-field reading; multi-field rapid-turn trajectories are not excluded.
(CG.12) What selects (b2, b3) = (12, 43)

Joyce's construction from phi's (Z/2)^3 reaches the family of CG.7; pi_1 is finite exactly on the n = 3 line, so on the compact form the holonomy is exactly G2 there and nowhere else in the family (CG.4). On that line the 12 bridges match the 12 A1 components as one 3 x 4 structure on 280 all-plain classes and on none of the 84 Example-4 classes; with WA-1 (one bridge = one resolved A1 component, adopted 2026-10-01) this selects (12, 43) without using data, the seed in force.

an all-plain n = 3 class other than (12, 43), a bijection on an Example-4 class, or finite pi_1 off the n = 3 line. Scope: WA-1 and the compact real form adopted 2026-10-01 (D-015); both are switches, so the split form and the ruling-only selection stay runnable.
